summary: Hippomenes was a Boeotian prince, the son of Megareus, who married Atalanta, the virginal runner, after defeating her in a footrace with the help of Aphrodite. According to the myth, he was given three golden apples that he dropped during the race to delay Atalanta and win her hand. He and Atalanta were later transformed into lions when they offended the gods by lying together in a sacred precinct. He is a distinct figure from the Arcadian Melanion, with whom he is often identified as Atalanta's husband.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: According to Ovid's Metamorphoses and Hyginus's Fabulae, Hippomenes was the son of King Megareus of Onchestus and his wife Merope. His genealogy belongs to the Boeotian version of the Atalanta myth, rooting him in a specific regional tradition.

Through his father he is given a noble descent: Ovid traces his line back to the god Neptune (Poseidon). His enduring connection in myth is to Atalanta, the swift-footed huntress whom he wins and marries.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: Footrace — Atalanta, wishing to avoid marriage despite her father's wishes, set a condition that she would marry only a suitor who could outrun her in a footrace; those who lost were put to death, in some accounts beheaded with their heads displayed in the stadium. Hippomenes at first mocked the fallen suitors as foolish, but when he saw Atalanta race naked he was overcome and offered himself as a contestant.

Aphrodite, moved by his daring, gave him three golden apples — said to come either from her sacred ground in Cyprus or from the Hesperides. During the race, whenever Atalanta began to draw ahead, Hippomenes dropped one of the apples; she paused to retrieve each one, and with Aphrodite making the last apple heavier, Hippomenes reached the finish first and won her as his wife.

Later life — Afterward Hippomenes failed to give proper thanks to Aphrodite. As the couple passed a sanctuary sacred to either Zeus or Cybele, the offended deity filled them with overwhelming desire, and they lay together within the sacred precinct. As punishment for the desecration the deity transformed them both into lions. In the version featuring Cybele, the goddess then yoked the pair to her chariot to draw it forever. Nonnus instead attributes their transformation to Artemis.
Notably, although other authors name Melanion as the father of Atalanta's son Parthenopaeus, no surviving source identifies Hippomenes as the boy's father.

sections.heading: Interpretation
paragraphs: Versions — The earliest attested version appears in a fragment of the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women, in which Atalanta yields to Hippomenes's plea and accepts the 'gifts of golden Aphrodite'; a scholiast reports that Hesiod showed Hippomenes racing naked. Hippomenes belongs to the Boeotian tradition while Melanion derives from Arcadian sources, and scholars debate whether they were originally distinct figures or variant names for one. Hippomenes appears only in the footrace and lion-transformation stories, never in Atalanta's other adventures such as the Calydonian boar hunt or the Argonautic voyage. The oldest attestation of the lion metamorphosis actually involves Melanion, and Apollodorus was the first to combine Melanion with the footrace; Apollodorus also describes Hippomenes as a hunter. The Arcadian Melanion, by contrast, wins Atalanta through devotion and 'great labour,' accompanying her on hunts, carrying her gear, and suffering wounds from harassing centaurs.

Sexuality and marriage — Theocritus depicts Atalanta falling in love with Hippomenes after her defeat, whereas Ovid shows her drawn to him beforehand. Footraces functioned as nuptial rites, especially in festivals honouring Hera, goddess of marriage, and contests in which a maiden's hand is the prize recur in Greek myth, though usually the father rather than the bride confronts the suitors. The race also mirrors a hunt, with Atalanta pursuing Hippomenes and so reversing the usual gender roles until she yields. The Greeks invested apples with meanings of sexuality and fertility, sacred to both Hera and Aphrodite; the Greek word for 'apple' covered other fruits such as pomegranate and quince, likewise treated as tokens of love, as in the myths of Persephone and of Cydippe, where accepting fruit seals a marriage bond. Because Atalanta resists marriage, her union comes only through conquest and defeat, yet the marriage remains 'wild,' with her still ranging the wilderness on the hunt.

Lions — It is hard to determine whether the lion-transformation myth originated in the Boeotian or the Arcadian tradition, since the archaic footrace tradition is poorly recorded and the couple's earlier Boeotian fate may have been different. Palaephatus rationalised the myth by proposing that the pair entered a lions' cave and were killed there, the lions afterward emerging and convincing their companions that the couple had been transformed. Hyginus, possibly following Pliny, and later Latin authors held that lions and lionesses could not mate with each other, so the lovers were punished by becoming animals abhorrent to Aphrodite; the Cybele version may reflect this, since her other servants and priests were similarly sexless or castrated. Adrienne Mayor disputes that lion sexlessness was a widespread ancient Greek belief, interpreting the transformation instead as placing Atalanta and Hippomenes beyond Greek social and cultural bounds.
